result.summary: Pausanias opens Book 9 with Bœotia, its name and the Platæans. He recounts their early history, their part against Xerxes, and their two expulsions, ending with Thebes razing Platæa and Philip later restoring it.

scenes.title: Platæa in the Persian and Greek wars

scenes.title: Thebes seizes Platæa
scenes.summary: Neocles leads the Thebans by a roundabout route and takes Platæa while its farmers are in the fields. The Platæans are expelled and the town razed, and Athens takes them in.
scenes.stakes: The Platæans lose their city and homes.

scenes.title: Philip restores Platæa
scenes.summary: After Chæronea Philip garrisons Thebes and restores the Platæans.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses both names for the people of Sparta.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias notes that early Greece was ruled by kings, with no democracies.

analysis.text: Pausanias traces Bœotian places to eponymous founders and shows how Platæa's fortunes rose and fell with Greek power struggles.
The passage records the fourth-century conflict between Thebes and Sparta and Athens, ending with Macedonian dominance under Philip.

fun_facts.text: Platæa was famous for the Greek victory over Mardonius in 479 BC, though Pausanias here mentions it only briefly.

language_notes.text: "Contiguous" means bordering; Bœotia adjoins Attica, and Platæa lies next to Eleutheræ, a town on the Attic border.
The Peace of Antalcidas (387 BC), also called the King's Peace, ended the Corinthian War on terms set by the Persian king.
Cadmea was Thebes' citadel, seized by a Spartan force in 382 BC; the Platæans claim they had no part in that plot.
A Bœotarch was one of the chief officers of the Bœotian league, here serving at Thebes.
"One dress" for men and "two" for women means each could carry off only the clothing specified, no other goods.
"Rased" is an old spelling of razed, meaning leveled; "no sack" means the town was not plundered.

context_notes.text: Platæa fought beside Athens at Marathon in 490 BC. Mardonius was defeated near Platæa in 479 BC, in the decisive land battle of the Persian invasion.
Leuctra (371 BC) was Thebes' great victory over Sparta; Platæa fell three years later, so about 373 BC by this reckoning.
Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chæronea in 338 BC and punished Thebes by favouring its enemies.

literary_notes.text: The phrase "destined to come upon them" hints that another disaster is coming for Platæa, preparing the account of the Theban attack.
Neocles is shown as shrewd: he notices the Platæans' routine and plans a roundabout march to exploit it.
The contrast between being shut in and being shut out sets the two disasters side by side to compare them.
